title: Leg 56 — Hoback Canyon to Pinedale Foothills
subtitle: Hoback Canyon, Bondurant, the Wind River front and Pinedale
preflightBriefing: Welcome aboard. We are leaving Jackson Hole and heading south into Hoback Canyon, then following the river country toward Bondurant before opening onto the Upper Green River basin. The Wind River Range will build along the left side as we continue toward Pinedale. Along the way there is fur-trade history, whitewater and wildlife country, a tiny church paid for with a diamond, one of North America's great wildlife migrations, working-ranch traditions, mountain tourism, and the old Green River rendezvous story. I'll stay quiet while you taxi and depart. Once you're airborne and settled, say Trip continue.

blocks.title: Leaving Jackson Hole
blocks.text: Jackson Hole is dropping behind as we head south. The Tetons will begin sliding toward the rear while the valley narrows toward Hoback Junction, where the Hoback River meets the Snake. The change from broad resort valley to river canyon happens quickly here.

blocks.title: Hoback Junction
blocks.text: Hoback Junction is coming up ahead. It is a small highway crossroads, but geographically it marks a clean transition: the Hoback arrives from the southeast, joins the Snake, and U.S. 191 turns into the canyon beside the river.

blocks.title: A nationally protected river system
blocks.text: The river country around this junction is part of the protected Snake River headwaters system. The designation recognizes not just scenery, but the connected fish, wildlife and recreation values of these mountain rivers.

blocks.title: Into Hoback Canyon
blocks.text: We are entering Hoback Canyon now, with the river and highway sharing the same narrow corridor. U.S. 191 follows the Hoback for miles through forested slopes and exposed rock, and on the ground this is part of Wyoming's Centennial Scenic Byway.

blocks.title: The man behind the name
blocks.text: The Hoback name comes from John Hoback, a Kentucky trapper who joined Wilson Price Hunt's Astorian expedition in 1811. Hoback and two companions helped guide the party across this part of Wyoming on its difficult overland journey toward the Columbia River.

blocks.title: A river for boaters
blocks.text: The lower Hoback has become popular with whitewater kayakers and rafters. The Forest Service also describes the canyon as important winter range for bighorn sheep, elk, deer and moose, so the same narrow corridor serves both recreation and migrating wildlife.

blocks.title: A road squeezed beside a river
blocks.text: From the air, notice how little room the canyon gives the highway. River bends, road cuts and steep slopes keep trading places along the valley floor. It is one of those Wyoming drives where the transportation corridor is part of the scenery rather than separate from it.

blocks.title: The canyon begins to open
blocks.text: The canyon starts relaxing into broader country ahead. Forested walls give way to more open sage and ranchland, a good preview of the much larger basins farther south.

blocks.title: Early travelers through hard country
blocks.text: This valley was part of the country crossed by the Astorians in the early 1810s. Their expeditions helped connect the fur-trade world of the Missouri with the Pacific Northwest, but their journals make clear that these mountains were anything but an easy shortcut.

blocks.title: Bondurant ahead
blocks.text: Bondurant is still several miles ahead, tucked into the widening valley. It remains a tiny ranching community rather than a conventional town, which is part of why the valley still feels so open from the air.

blocks.title: A church paid for with a diamond
blocks.text: Bondurant has one of the better small-town stories in Wyoming. St. Hubert the Hunter church was financed with the sale of a donated diamond. Local ranchers cut the logs and supplied much of the labor, and the church was completed in 1941.

blocks.title: A barbecue that outgrew the town
blocks.text: The church dedication helped launch the annual Bondurant barbecue. The first one in 1941 drew more than five hundred people, far more than the community's permanent population, with visitors arriving by stagecoach and horseback as well as by road.

blocks.title: Out into broader Wyoming
blocks.text: South of Bondurant the country opens dramatically. Ranches, sagebrush and long mountain fronts replace the tight canyon, and the view begins to feel more like the vast interior Wyoming basin country.

blocks.title: A migration older than the roads
blocks.text: This broader region is crossed by the Path of the Pronghorn. Animals move between summer range in Grand Teton National Park and winter range in the Upper Green River basin, following a migration that has been used for thousands of years.

blocks.title: Built for open country
blocks.text: Pronghorn fit this landscape perfectly. They are North America's fastest land animals and can sprint around sixty miles an hour. Unlike deer, they are reluctant jumpers, so fences can be a bigger obstacle than a wide open stretch of sage.

blocks.title: The Wind Rivers take over the left side
blocks.text: The Wind River Range should now be becoming the dominant mountain wall off the left side. The range stretches for roughly a hundred miles and contains Wyoming's highest summit, Gannett Peak, along with a remarkable concentration of high alpine lakes and glaciers.

blocks.title: A backcountry magnet
blocks.text: For hikers and climbers, the Winds are one of the great backcountry destinations in the Rockies. Pinedale is a primary western gateway, with trailheads leading into places such as Titcomb Basin and the Bridger Wilderness. Many visitors come specifically for multi-day trips far from roads and cell service.

blocks.title: A cattle drive still happening
blocks.text: Ranching traditions are still visible here too. The Green River Drift began in the 1890s and continues as cattle are moved between winter range and high summer grazing. Local tourism promoters describe it as the country's longest-running cattle drive.

blocks.title: Along the west face of the Winds
blocks.text: The Wind River Range remains off the left side now, with the broad basin giving you room to read the mountain front as a single wall. More than forty named peaks in the range rise above thirteen thousand feet.

blocks.title: Where the Green River begins
blocks.text: Farther north in these mountains, the Green River begins near Green River Lakes beneath Squaretop Mountain. From here it eventually joins the Colorado River system, linking this quiet Wyoming basin to water users hundreds of miles downstream.

blocks.title: Pinedale country ahead
blocks.text: Pinedale is coming into the picture ahead. It is small, but it serves as a major gateway for the western Wind Rivers, with outfitters, trailheads, climbing access and a local identity that leans heavily on both ranching and the old mountain-man era.

blocks.title: Pinedale ahead
blocks.text: Pinedale is still roughly eight miles ahead. The town sits west of the Wind River front, with Fremont Lake just beyond it toward the mountains. The open basin makes even a small community stand out clearly from the air.

blocks.title: A bottleneck used for thousands of years
blocks.text: West of Pinedale is Trapper's Point, where the Green and New Fork rivers squeeze migration paths through a natural bottleneck. Archaeological work there has found evidence that people were hunting pronghorn in this corridor thousands of years ago.

blocks.title: When the mountain men came to trade
blocks.text: The Upper Green became one of the centers of the Rocky Mountain fur trade. Several famous rendezvous were held near here in the 1830s, when trappers, traders and Native people gathered to exchange furs and supplies, settle accounts, socialize and tell stories.

blocks.title: Pinedale keeps the rendezvous tradition alive
blocks.text: Pinedale still celebrates that history every July with the Green River Rendezvous. The modern event mixes living-history demonstrations with a parade, rodeo, music and plenty of deliberate mountain-man theatricality.

blocks.title: A small museum with a big local identity
blocks.spokenLabel: the Museum of the Mountain Man
blocks.text: The Museum of the Mountain Man is one of Pinedale's signature attractions and draws about twelve thousand visitors during its six-month season. Its collection includes Jim Bridger's rifle and artifacts from the fur-trade era.

blocks.title: Pinedale below
blocks.text: Pinedale should be close below now. It is the kind of town whose scale makes more sense from the air: a compact community surrounded by enormous stretches of ranchland, sage and mountain country.

blocks.title: Ralph Wenz Field
blocks.text: Ralph Wenz Field lies southeast of town. The airport began as a grass strip in the late 1940s and is named for Ralph Wenz, a local Army Air Corps navigator who worked on cold-weather equipment testing in Alaska before his death in a 1947 aircraft accident.
